questions.question: Read the passage on computers and 'automation', then answer: state the two main functions of computers.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** According to the passage, computers have two main functions:

1. **To solve the most complex mathematical problems** — "They can solve the most complex mathematical problems".
2. **To put thousands of unrelated data in order** — "or put thousand data in order".

**How to score full marks here.** The question asks for *two* functions, so give both in one line each and quote the passage's own words where possible. Do not add functions the passage does not mention (e.g. "control human beings"), since the passage explicitly denies that computers can do so.

**Supporting detail (optional, if a little extra is wanted).** The passage also says computers "work accurately and at high speed" and "save research workers' years of hard work" — these are *qualities* of the two functions, not separate functions.

questions.question: Read the passage on computers and 'automation', then answer: what is automation?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The passage defines automation as **the process by which machines can be used to work for human beings**:

> "This whole process by which machines can be used to work for us has been called 'Automation'."

**Explanation in your own words.** Automation means handing over work — calculation, data handling, checking records — to machines that carry it out automatically, so that human effort is replaced or reduced.

**What the passage adds about its effect.** Automation is expected to "enable human beings to enjoy more leisure than they do today", and its coming is "bound to have important social consequences". Mentioning one of these shows a full reading of the paragraph, but the definition is the mark-earning part.

questions.question: Read the passage on computers and 'automation', then answer: what benefit can man derive from 'automation'?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The benefits stated in the passage are:

1. **Relief from heavy mental labour** — if machines work for human beings, "lots of data-processing and calculation work are automated", so people are spared years of hard work.
2. **More leisure** — "Human beings have more leisure", because the dull clerical and computing work is done by machines.
3. **Better services in daily life** — computers can supply information about the weather, suggest alternative routes in a traffic jam, translate languages, and keep patients' health records up to date.

**Model two-mark answer (what to write in the paper).** Automation relieves human beings of tedious calculation and clerical work, giving them more leisure, and it provides accurate, speedy information and services in areas such as weather forecasting, traffic, translation and hospital records.

**Careful distinction.** The question asks for *benefit*, so do not write about the dangers or the "social consequences" — those belong to a different part of the passage.

questions.question: Read the passage on computers and 'automation', then answer: what is the basic limitation of computers?
Read the passage on computers and 'automation', then answer: mention two areas in which computers can be effectively used.
Find the antonyms of the following words from the given passage: (i) Easy (Para-1) (ii) Same (Para-3).
questions.answer:
**Answers.**

| Word | Antonym (from the passage) |
|---|---|
| (i) **Easy** | **complex** |
| (ii) **Same** | **alternative** |

**Where they occur.**

- Para 1: "They can solve the most **complex** mathematical problems" — *complex* is the opposite of *easy*.
- Para 3: "Car drivers can be given an **alternative** route, when there is a traffic jam" — an *alternative* route is a *different* (not the same) route.

**How to find antonyms from a passage.** Scan for the word and read the whole sentence: the antonym is usually the contrast word in the same clause ("complex" answers "easy", "alternative" answers "same"). Do not invent a synonym of your own — the paper requires the word *from the passage*, and marks are lost if the word does not appear there.

**Note on the printed key.** The booklet gives "(a) complex (b) Alternative", which agrees with the analysis above.

questions.question: Read the passage on Information Technology and libraries, and make notes on it using headings and subheadings. Also give an appropriate title.
questions.answer:
**Title: Information Technology and Library Services**

**1. Library and IT — complementary**
   (i) Two faces of the same coin
   (ii) Both cater to education, information, recreation

**2. Library as an instrument of social change**
   (i) Old view: library = books, librarian = keeper of books
   (ii) New view: multimedia centre, place of learning resources
   (iii) Serves the literate and the illiterate
   (iv) Education — key to individual achievement, national strength

**3. Village scenario**
   (i) Young and old use the library; the middle-aged use it little
   (ii) Middle-aged need job-related information, skill and knowledge update

**4. Integrated approach — the need of the hour**
   (i) At least one reading room in every hamlet
   (ii) Co-ordination between Dept. of Education and Panchayati Raj
   (iii) Amalgamation of adult education programmes with library programmes
   (iv) School to serve as library in a hamlet/village
   (v) One house for every 1,000 houses (or cluster) earmarked for library
   (vi) Service of a retired teacher/employee — more useful than an outsider
   (vii) Library to function in the evening, extended to TV and Internet

**5. Role of Information Technology, Internet and e-commerce**
   (i) Great potential for public needs
   (ii) Pragmatic approach needed in rural areas
   (iii) Five requirements: Availability, Affordability, Accessibility, Acceptability, Sustainability
   (iv) Common service place — IT services can be "cushioned on"

**6. Conclusion**
   (i) State and central governments to give top priority
   (ii) Aim: an enhanced minimum facility for all

**Marking scheme reminder.** Notes must use **headings and sub-headings** with abbreviated points (not full sentences); the **title** carries a mark of its own. Keep the numbering consistent (1, 2, 3 … and (i), (ii) …) — this is what the examiner looks for after the content.

questions.question: Write a summary of the above passage (on Information Technology and libraries) in about 50 words.
questions.answer:
**Summary (about 50 words).**

Information Technology and library services are complementary and together serve the educational, informational and recreational needs of society. The modern library, no longer a mere store of books, should become a multimedia learning centre. The need of the hour is a reading room in every hamlet, with government support making IT services available, affordable and sustainable in rural areas.

**Why this is a good summary.**

- It keeps only the **main ideas**: the two services are complementary; the library's changed role; the village-level plan; IT in rural areas; the government's role.
- It drops examples and statistics (1,000 houses, retired teachers, e-commerce details).
- It is written in **continuous prose** (a summary must not be a list of notes) and stays close to the 50-word limit.

**Technique worth remembering.** For a 50-word summary of a six-paragraph passage, allot roughly one sentence to the opening claim, one to the changed concept, and one to the recommendation — anything more will exceed the limit and earn no extra marks.

questions.question: You are President of the Cultural Society of your college/school. You are planning to organise a cultural programme. Write a notice for the college/school notice board, inviting names of students willing to participate. Sign yourself as ABC of XYZ School/College, Ranchi. (Word limit 50 words)
questions.answer:
**NOTICE**

**XYZ SCHOOL/COLLEGE, RANCHI**
**CULTURAL SOCIETY**

**3 August 2012**

**CULTURAL PROGRAMME — INVITATION FOR PARTICIPATION**

The Cultural Society is organising a cultural evening on 3 September 2012 at 5 p.m. in the school auditorium. Items include solo song, group dance, skit, elocution and instrumental music. Students of Classes IX–XII who wish to participate may give their names to the undersigned by 20 August 2012.

ABC
President, Cultural Society

**Format checklist (what fetches the marks).**

1. The word **NOTICE** at the top, centred.
2. **Name of the institution** and the issuing body (Cultural Society).
3. **Date** of issue.
4. A **short heading/caption** in capitals.
5. **Body**: what, when, where, who may participate, and the **last date** for names.
6. **Signature and designation** of the writer at the bottom left.
7. Kept **within 50 words** and inside a box — a notice is always displayed in a box on the board.

**Common mistakes to avoid:** writing it as a letter (no "Dear students", no salutation), forgetting the date, or giving your home address — a notice carries only the issuing authority.

questions.question: Your neighbour Satish wants to seek admission in XI class in your school/college. He does not know much about the procedure regarding admission to a school/college. Being a student of the senior class of your school/college, describe him the procedure of 'Admission to a College/School'. (Word limit 125 words)
questions.answer:
**Examination Hall, Ranchi**
**25 March 2012**

**Dear Satish**

I am very happy to learn that you wish to join Class XI in our school. Let me explain the procedure.

First, collect the admission form from the school office on any working day between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. and fill it in carefully, attaching a photograph, your Class X marksheet and a transfer certificate. Submit it before the last date announced on the notice board. You will then have to appear for a short entrance test in English, Mathematics and General Science. If you qualify, your name will be displayed on the notice board, and you will be called for a brief interview with the Principal along with your parents. After the fee is deposited, you will be allotted a section and issued an identity card.

Do let me know if you need any help with the form.

**Yours sincerely**
**Abhishek**

**Format checklist.**

- Sender's address and **date** at the top; no address of the receiver in an informal letter.
- Salutation "Dear Satish" (first name only), then the body in **three short paragraphs** (purpose — procedure in sequence — closing).
- Complimentary close "Yours sincerely" (not "Your's" or "Yours faithfully", which belongs to formal letters) and the writer's name.
- The steps must be in **logical order**: form → documents → test → result → interview → fee → section.

**Note on the printed answer.** The booklet's model answer is shorter than the word limit and ends "Yours sincerely / Abhishek"; the version above keeps the same facts but fills the 125-word requirement.

questions.question: Write a report in about 125 words on a One-Day Cricket Match played by your college/school against ABC school/college, Ranchi.
questions.answer:
**ONE-DAY CRICKET MATCH: KAMLA NEHRU VIDYALAYA BEAT GANDHI SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL**

**By a Staff Reporter / Our Correspondent**
**Giridih, 20 December 2010**

A one-day cricket match was played yesterday between Kamla Nehru Vidyalaya, Giridih, and Gandhi Senior Secondary School, Ranchi, on the Vidyalaya ground. A large crowd, including students of both schools, gathered an hour before the match.

Kamla Nehru won the toss and elected to bat. After a shaky start, in which they lost three quick wickets, Mukesh and Gandhi put on a century partnership and took the total to a respectable 230. Gandhi's opening spell then rattled the Ranchi side, whose batsmen collapsed for 190 runs. The spinners tightened the grip in the middle overs, and the last five wickets fell for only thirty runs.

Kamla Nehru Vidyalaya won by 40 runs. Mukesh was declared Man of the Match. The Principal congratulated both teams and gave away the prizes.

**Format checklist for a report.**

1. A **headline** in capitals (a report is read, not displayed, so it may be in sentence case too).
2. **By-line** (reporter's name/designation) and **place-date line**.
3. **Opening paragraph** answering what, where, when, who.
4. **Middle paragraphs** giving the sequence of the match — toss, innings, turning points, scores.
5. **Closing paragraph** with the result and any remarks or prizes.
6. Written in the **third person and past tense**, without "I" or "we" — a report is impersonal.

**Why the details must be specific.** A report is judged on factual texture: names, scores, the turning point, and the margin of victory. Vague statements such as "it was a good match" carry no marks.

questions.question: The Government has banned smoking in public places. Write an article on 'Hazards of Smoking' in about 150 words for your school magazine. You are Anu, of XII A.
questions.answer:
**SMOKING AND ITS HAZARDS**

**by Anu, XII A**

Smoking is a slow poison that eats away the human body. It is most prevalent among the young, who take to a cigarette for fun and adventure and then find it very difficult to give up.

The harm begins at once. Tobacco contains nicotine, which impairs the digestive system, and tar, which damages the lungs. Smoking causes cancer of the mouth, the throat, the tongue and the lungs, and it weakens the heart. Millions of people die of smoking-related diseases every year, especially in the developing countries, where awareness is low.

The Government has therefore banned smoking in public places — cinema halls, hospitals, railway stations, schools and colleges. This step alone, however, will not be effective unless people, and especially the young, are awakened to the hazards of smoking. Mass media, television and radio must carry advertisements that persuade people to quit.

All young people should take a sincere pledge never to smoke. Life is there to be lived, not to be ruined by our own bad habits.

**Format checklist for an article.**

1. **Title** at the top, followed by the writer's name and class (as asked: "You are Anu, of XII A").
2. An **introduction** stating the problem and its importance.
3. Two or three **body paragraphs**, each with one clear idea — the physical harm, then the social measures.
4. A **conclusion** that appeals to the reader (a pledge, a resolve).
5. Formal, impersonal tone; rhetorical questions and short sentences are effective here, but slang is not.

**Content to include for full marks:** the diseases named in the paper's own source passage (mouth, throat, tongue, lungs, digestion), the ban on smoking in public places, and the role of the media and of self-discipline.

questions.question: Read the extract from the poem beginning ‘Driving from my parents' home to Cochin last Friday morning…’ and answer: name the poem and the poet.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

- **Poem:** "My Mother at Sixty-Six"
- **Poet:** **Kamala Das**

**Context.** The extract describes the poet driving from her parents' home to Cochin, with her ageing mother dozing beside her. It is a single-sentence poem: the sight of her mother's face — "ashen like that of a corpse" — reminds the poet of her mother's approaching death, a thought she pushes away and hides behind a cheerful goodbye.

**One mark, one line.** Since the question carries a single mark, only the two names are required; no explanation is needed, and adding one costs time that other questions need.

questions.question: Read the extract from the poem beginning ‘Driving from my parents' home to Cochin last Friday morning…’ and answer: what did she notice while her mother sat beside her?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** She noticed that her mother was **dozing with her mouth open, her face pale and ashen "like that of a corpse"**.

**The exact words of the extract:**

> "…I saw my mother beside me / doze, open mouthed, her face ashen like that of a corpse…"

**What makes the observation painful.** The mother's face has lost its colour and youth; the open mouth and slack features of sleep make her look, for an instant, like a dead body. That is why the poet "realised with pain" that her mother was old and near the end of life.

**One-mark answer.** The poet noticed that her mother, sitting beside her in the car, was dozing with her mouth open and her face ashen, like a corpse.

questions.question: Read the extract from the poem beginning ‘Driving from my parents' home to Cochin last Friday morning…’ and answer: what thought did she put away?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** She put away the **thought of her mother's approaching death** — the fear that this might be the last time she saw her alive.

**How the poem words it.** The sight of her mother's "ashen" face, "like that of a corpse", brings the realisation "with pain" that her mother is old and will soon die. To escape the thought, the poet "looked out at young / Trees sprinting, the merry children spilling / out of their homes" — images of life and energy that push the idea of death out of her mind.

**Why she puts it away.** She cannot bear to face it, and she does not want to weep before her mother. So she hides the thought and, at the airport, only says what she has always said:

> "…all I did was smile and smile and smile…"

The repeated "smile" is the mask she puts on the pain.

**Full two-mark answer.** The poet put away the painful thought of her mother's old age and imminent death, which the mother's corpse-like face had forced upon her. She turned her eyes to the young trees and the merry children, symbols of life, and hid her fear behind a repeated smile at the airport — a smile that conceals an ache she cannot express.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: why was the mother compared to the 'Late winter's moon'?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The late winter's moon looks pale, dim and lifeless, its brightness nearly spent. The mother, at sixty-six, has the same faded, ashen look — her youth and strength gone. The comparison therefore conveys her old age and nearness to death.

**Unpacked (what the examiner rewards).**

- A late-winter moon is **wan, hazy and colourless** — it has lost the glow of other seasons.
- The mother's face is similarly **"ashen"**, pale and dim, drained of the vitality it once had.
- Winter itself suggests the **last season of life**, so the image quietly announces approaching death.

**Model 35-word answer.** She is like the late winter's moon — pale, dim and shorn of brightness. Old age has drained the colour and strength from her face, leaving the ashen look of a life near its winter's end.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what will counting up to twelve and keeping still help us achieve?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Counting to twelve and keeping still gives us a moment of silence in which to stop, think and look within. It lets us understand ourselves and others, and prevents the hasty, thoughtless actions that cause most of our troubles.

**Why the poet asks for this.** Neruda believes that "most of our difficulties and troubles stem because we rush through a thing and hurry to do things without considering their consequences". The count of twelve is a device to break that rush — a short, universal pause in which everybody on earth is silent at the same time.

**Model 35-word answer.** It gives us a rare moment of stillness in which to reflect instead of rushing into action. Such self-examination would end the hurry and thoughtlessness that breed most of our difficulties and troubles.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what makes human beings love life in spite of troubles and sufferings?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Beautiful things — "a thing of beauty" — do. They lift our spirits, remove the pall of gloom from our minds and bind us to the earth, so that despite pain and suffering we go on loving life.

**The poet's argument.** Keats says that "some shape of beauty" — a flower, a stream, the sun, the moon, a tale of mighty dead — "moves away the pall / From our dark spirits". Because beauty is a "joy for ever", it renews our will to live each time sorrow threatens to overwhelm us.

**Model 35-word answer.** The presence of beautiful things around us makes us love life. Their loveliness drives away the gloom that troubles and sufferings cast on our minds, and fills us with a quiet, lasting joy.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what was the temptation and how did Franz resist it?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The temptation was to skip school. The day was warm and bright, birds were chirping and Prussian soldiers were drilling in the open field — all far more attractive than a lesson on participles. But Franz resisted and hurried to school.

**Why he was tempted.** He was late and afraid of being scolded, for M. Hamel had said he would question the class on participles, of which Franz "knew nothing". Nature and the drill offered an easy escape.

**How he resisted.** He "had the strength to resist", telling himself it was "warm, bright", yet he "hurried off to school". The will to face the scolding wins — and that decision saves him from missing the last French lesson of his life.

**Model 35-word answer.** Franz was tempted to spend the day out of doors — it was warm and bright, birds were chirping and soldiers drilling — and to escape M. Hamel's feared questions on participles. Yet he overcame the urge and hurried to school.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: who was Saheb? What was his full name? What was the irony about his name?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Saheb was a ragpicker of Seemapuri. His full name was **Saheb-e-Alam**, meaning "lord of the universe". The irony is that this lord of the universe scrounges for gold in garbage dumps and walks barefoot.

**The irony spelled out.**

- A name that claims **universal lordship** belongs to a boy who owns nothing — no shoes, no school, no certain meal.
- He is free in name ("lord") but bound by poverty, and his "gold" is what others throw away.

**Model 35-word answer.** Saheb was a young ragpicker of Seemapuri whose full name, Saheb-e-Alam, means "lord of the universe". The irony is bitter: this lord of the universe scrounges in garbage dumps for a living and owns almost nothing.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: why was Douglas determined to get over his fear of water?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The fear had spoilt his life. It ruined his fishing trips, kept him out of the water and deprived him of canoeing, boating and swimming. He was determined to conquer it and enjoy these pleasures like anyone else.

**In the author's words.** "It [the fear] deprived me of the joy of canoeing, boating and swimming." Whenever he tried to enter a lake or river, "the terror that had seized me in the pool would come back", and he "used every way he knew to overcome this fear".

**How he did it.** He engaged an instructor, practised until he could swim the length of the pool and across Lake Wentworth, and thus "conquered" the fear — proof that determination can defeat even the deepest terror.

**Model 35-word answer.** Douglas was determined to overcome his fear because it had ruined his fishing trips and robbed him of the joy of canoeing, boating and swimming. He wanted to enjoy the water as others did, free of terror.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what made the peddler think that he had indeed fallen into a rattrap?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The ironmaster mistook him for an old comrade and took him home. The peddler thought of the thirty kronor he had stolen and of the ironmaster's invitation to a manor house — and felt he had walked into the rattrap himself.

**The chain of thought in the story.** The peddler had always said the world was a rattrap: "baits" of food, shelter and money lay about, and once a man took the bait "there was no escape". Now he was fed, clothed and offered shelter — the cheese was tempting — and he recalled the crofter's thirty kronor in his pocket.

**Model 35-word answer.** Now that the ironmaster had taken him home, clothed and fed him, the peddler felt he had himself walked into the trap. The thought of the thirty kronor he had stolen made him fear the manor was the bait.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: how was Gandhi able to influence lawyers? Give instance.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** By his own example of self-sacrifice. When lawyers charged high fees from poor sharecroppers, Gandhi rebuked them, and when they feared jail he said he alone would go to prison for the peasants. Ashamed, they agreed to follow him.

**The instance in detail.** At Motihari, the lawyers were collecting big fees from sharecroppers. Gandhi told them it was "shameless" to do so when the peasants were "so crushed". A peasant asked what would happen if Gandhi went to jail — who would fight for them then? The lawyers felt ashamed, and "when they saw that Gandhi was prepared to go to jail for the peasants, they were touched" and agreed to court arrest.

**Model 35-word answer.** Gandhi influenced the lawyers by practising what he preached. He told them that charging heavy fees to poor sharecroppers was shameful and declared he alone would go to jail for the peasants; moved, they pledged to follow him.

questions.question: Answer any one of the following in about 125 words: Who was Rajkumar Shukla? How did he take Gandhiji to Champaran and why?
questions.answer:
**Rajkumar Shukla** was a poor, illiterate peasant sharecropper from Champaran in Bihar. Thin, weak and poorly clad even in December, he came to the Lucknow Congress session of 1916 to complain about the injustice of the landlord system — in Champaran most of the arable land was owned by English landlords who forced the Indian sharecroppers to grow indigo. Someone had advised him to meet Gandhi.

Gandhi had appointments in Kanpur and elsewhere, but Shukla would not be put off. He followed Gandhi everywhere, never leaving his side, and begged him to fix a date. Impressed by his tenacity and devotion, Gandhi asked him to come to Calcutta. Months later, Shukla was waiting at Gandhi's ashram when Gandhi reached Calcutta; then the two boarded a train to Patna.

**Why Shukla did all this.** He wanted the peasants' grievances heard by someone powerful enough to fight the British landlords. For him, Gandhi was the only hope of justice for thousands of sharecroppers who had no voice of their own.

**Why the detail matters in the story.** Shukla's persistence is what brings Gandhi to Champaran: a single determined peasant sets in motion the first satyagraha in India.

**Model 125-word answer.** Rajkumar Shukla was a poor, illiterate sharecropper from Champaran, Bihar, who came to the 1916 Lucknow Congress session to complain about the landlords' injustice — the English planters forced the peasants to grow indigo and took most of the profit. Someone advised him to meet Gandhi. Though Gandhi had other engagements, Shukla followed him everywhere for weeks and begged him to fix a date. Touched by such persistence, Gandhi told him to come to Calcutta; Shukla was waiting there for months, and the two then boarded a train to Patna. Shukla did this because the sharecroppers had no one to speak for them; he wanted the injustice ended, and he saw in Gandhi the one leader willing to fight for the poor.

questions.question: Answer any one of the following in about 125 words: Describe the make-up department of the Gemini Studios. How did it prepare the players for a movie?
questions.answer:
The make-up department of Gemini Studios was on the first floor of what had once been Robert Clive's stables. Its room looked like a "hair-cutting saloon" and had half a dozen large mirrors; incandescent lights fitted at all angles radiated so much heat that the atmosphere was "very hot and unpleasant". Inside, a strict hierarchy ruled: the chief make-up man made the chief actors and actresses "ugly", his senior assistant made the "second" hero and heroine ugly, the junior assistant made the "second" comedian ugly, and the office-boy was responsible for the crowd players.

The department thus turned ordinary men and women into the faces a film needed. With truckloads of pancake, and locally made lotions and potions, the staff could make a "decent looking person into a hideous monster" — or age a young actor, darken a complexion, or produce a wound. It was, in the narrator's words, a picture of national integration too: a Bengali, a Maharashtrian, a Kannadiga, an Andhra and local Tamils worked together.

**Model 125-word answer.** The make-up department of Gemini Studios occupied the first floor of what was believed to be Robert Clive's stables. Its room resembled a hair-cutting saloon, with half a dozen large mirrors, and the incandescent lights arranged at all angles made the place very hot and unpleasant. A strict hierarchy worked there: the chief make-up man made the heroes and heroines "ugly", the senior assistant handled the second lead, the junior assistant the comedian, and the office-boy the crowd. Using truckloads of pancake and locally made lotions and potions, they could turn a decent-looking person into a hideous monster, ageing or disfiguring faces as the script required. The staff came from Bengal, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra and Tamil Nadu.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: Answer any one of the following in about 125 words: What do you know about the geological history of Gondwana? How did the Antarctica become cold and barren?
questions.answer:
**Gondwana** was a giant southern super-continent that existed about 650 million years ago. India and Antarctica were parts of it, and what is now South America, Africa, Australia and Madagascar were joined with them in one landmass centred around present-day Antarctica. Human beings had not yet appeared. The climate was much warmer, and the region supported a huge variety of flora and fauna. Gondwana survived for about 500 million years.

Then geological disturbances forced the landmasses to separate and drift into countries as we know them today. India pushed northwards and collided with Asia, raising the Himalayas; South America drifted west to join North America. This movement created a cold circumpolar current that cut Antarctica off from warmer waters — the isolation "pushed Antarctica northwards" — and the continent became frigid and desolate. Today ninety per cent of the earth's ice volume is stored there, and it is a place to study ozone, carbon and extinction.

**Model 125-word answer.** About 650 million years ago a giant super-continent called Gondwana lay in the south, with India and Antarctica part of it and the present South America, Africa and Australia attached. No human being had appeared. Its climate was much warmer than now and it supported a vast variety of plants and animals, surviving some 500 million years. Geological disturbances then split it: India drifted north, collided with Asia and threw up the Himalayas, while South America joined North America. Antarctica was left alone at the pole, and a cold circumpolar current formed around it, sealing off warmer currents. Cut off and frozen, it turned into a frigid desert where ninety per cent of the world's ice is stored.

questions.question: Answer any one of the following in about 125 words: Will Dr Sadao take the man in and save him?
questions.answer:
Yes — Dr Sadao does take the wounded American prisoner in and save him, though only after a painful struggle between his duty as a doctor and his loyalty as a Japanese citizen in wartime.

When he finds the bleeding white man on the beach, his first instinct is professional: "the man will die" unless operated upon. He and Hana carry him home and lay him on a mat. Hana is terrified — harbouring an enemy is treason — yet she helps, washing the wound and holding the anaesthetic bottle while her husband operates. Sadao removes the bullet and the man survives.

Privately Sadao wavers: he could hand the prisoner over to the police, or let him escape. He chooses humanity. He tells the General about the man, and although the General promises to send assassins who never come, Sadao finally helps the prisoner escape by boat to a nearby island, with food, clothing and directions. Mercy, not patriotism, wins.

**Model 125-word answer.** Dr Sadao does take the man in and save him. Finding a wounded American prisoner of war on the beach, he cannot forget his oath as a doctor; to leave him would be to let him die. He and Hana carry the man home, and despite her fear of the punishment for sheltering an enemy, they operate and remove the bullet. Sadao's conflict is intense: as a Japanese he should hand the prisoner over; as a doctor he must heal him. He reports the matter to the General, who promises to send men, but no one comes. In the end Sadao chooses mercy. He gives the young man a boat, food and clothing and helps him escape to a nearby island, knowing the man will signal for help and be rescued.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: how did Charley reach the third level?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** One night Charley worked late at the office and, in a hurry to reach home, took the subway from Grand Central. He went down the steps to the first level, then lost his way in the growing maze of corridors and staircases, and found himself on the third level.

**How the story describes it.** "The Grand Central is growing like a tree, pushing out new corridors and staircases like roots." He was "lost" — and being lost on the subway is, he says, quite easy for anyone. So he wandered into a corridor that had no such thing as the third level. That is the fictional device: the third level is a doorway into 1894.

**Model 35-word answer.** Charley, hurrying home late one night, took the subway from Grand Central, went down to the first level and lost his way in its maze of corridors and staircases. Wandering on, he unexpectedly found himself on the third level.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what was the Maharaja's feeling when he killed the hundredth tiger?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He was overcome with **elation and triumph**. He had killed the hundredth tiger and so outlived the prophecy. He ordered the dead tiger to be brought to the capital in a grand procession, buried it, and had a tomb erected over it.

**Why such triumph?** Because the astrologer had foretold that his death would come from a tiger, and the Maharaja had spent years and a fortune killing ninety-nine of them. The hundredth kill, as he believed, defeated fate itself — hence the procession, the burial and the "monument" over the corpse.

**The irony.** The hundredth tiger, in fact, was not killed by him: it fainted at his shot and was finished off later by a hunter. The Maharaja died not of a tiger's attack but of an infection from a silver sliver in a cheap wooden toy tiger — so the prophecy was fulfilled in the most mocking way.

**Model 35-word answer.** The Maharaja was filled with elation. Believing he had killed the hundredth tiger and defeated the prophecy, he ordered it to be brought to the capital in a grand procession, buried it and raised a tomb over it.

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what is wrong with Derry's face? How do people react when they look at it?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** One side of Derry's face is badly burnt, so it is disfigured. People stare and then turn away, and some are cruel: a woman says, "Look at that, that's terrible," and others treat him as a freak.

**The details in the play.** Acid burnt his face when he was a child; he has "a face burned on one side". He tells Mr Lamb that people "look at me and then look away" — they either pity him or are repelled, and one woman's remark convinces him that he is ugly and unwanted. That is why he has become bitter and solitary.

**Model 35-word answer.** One side of Derry's face has been burnt by acid, leaving it disfigured. People stare, then quickly look away; some whisper or make cruel remarks, and a woman once said loudly, "Look at that, that's terrible."

questions.question: Answer in about 35 words: what kind of person was Evans?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Evans, "Evans the Break", was a jailbird who had escaped from prison three times. Cheerful, pleasant and good at imitations, he was never violent; his weakness was an incurable urge to steal — a disease he was born with.

**Details worth adding.** At the time of the story he was in a solitary cell in Oxford Prison. The prison officers had nicknamed him "Evans the Break" because of his escapes, and he was "a pleasant sort of chap, an amusing person" who "was good at imitations". He was "not at all violent" — he "suffered" from the compulsion to steal.

**Why the character matters.** Evans's pleasantness is precisely what makes him dangerous: the Governor underestimates him, and he escapes again — disguised, ironically, as the examination invigilator.

**Model 35-word answer.** Evans was a cheerful, pleasant jailbird nicknamed "Evans the Break" for his three escapes from prison. Good at imitations and never violent, he suffered from an incurable compulsion to steal — a disease, he claimed, he was born with.
